explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF sends row-count messages for statements in the procedure.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, some run-time errors can leave an explicit transaction open.
The customer filter is initialized to the fixed customer ID 1.
@OrderID is initialized to a fixed order ID rather than a caller-selected value.
SELECT * returns every Sales.Orders column, including large text columns, and makes the result shape depend on the table schema.
Without ORDER BY, SQL Server can return any ten order IDs.
Sales.Orders.OrderID is the primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any duplicates.
NOLOCK can return uncommitted rows or miss or duplicate rows during concurrent writes.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) makes the filter non-sargable; a date range can compare OrderDate directly.
The filter fixes the reporting year at 2016.
SQL Server implicitly converts @CustomerIdText from nvarchar to int to compare it with Orders.CustomerID.
The OR predicate combines an unfiltered query and a CustomerID lookup, which can lead to a plan that performs poorly for one case.
LIKE N'%urgent%' cannot use a prefix seek on Comments.
ISNULL wraps Orders.CustomerID and can prevent a direct seek on its index even though the column is NOT NULL.
The predicate embeds customer ID 1 as the only match.
Adding zero to OrderID is redundant and can prevent a direct primary-key seek.
CustomerID <> 1 may match most orders, limiting the usefulness of the CustomerID index.
The predicate excludes a fixed customer ID rather than taking the exclusion as input.
TOP (1) chooses an arbitrary order-customer pair.
CROSS JOIN pairs orders with unrelated customers because it does not match their CustomerID values.
TOP (1) does not specify which matching order to return.
The comma-separated FROM list puts the Orders-OrderLines join condition in WHERE rather than in an explicit JOIN.
The scalar count is correlated by OrderID and can require repeated OrderLines lookups.
The correlated EXISTS can probe OrderLines for each order; a join to a deduplicated set of qualifying OrderIDs would preserve the result.
The qualifying order-line quantity threshold is fixed at 1.
The CASE expression for HasComments is repeated in ORDER BY instead of using the select-list alias.
ORDER BY 2 silently changes meaning if the select-list position of OrderDate changes.
OrderDate is not unique, so orders tied at the page boundary can be selected inconsistently without an OrderID tie-breaker.
The first branch embeds order ID 1.
The branches return different primary-key values, so UNION's duplicate elimination is unnecessary.
The second branch embeds order ID 2.
COUNT(*) counts matching order lines even though the filter only needs to know whether one exists.
The unrestricted SELECT assigns @OrderID from an unspecified last row, making later uses of the value unpredictable.
The table variable receives an arbitrary set of five order IDs.
#ImplicitOrders receives an arbitrary set of five order IDs.
SELECT INTO derives the schema of #ImplicitOrders from the query rather than declaring it explicitly.
The cursor query takes two arbitrary orders, so its single FETCH can assign an unpredictable @OrderID.
The CustomerID query embeds the converted integer in SQL text instead of using a typed parameter.
EXEC runs the CustomerID query without binding its filter value, so different IDs produce different SQL text.
The OrderID query embeds the converted integer in SQL text instead of using a typed parameter.
The sp_executesql call supplies no parameter declaration or binding for OrderID.
#Scratch is not explicitly dropped and remains allocated until the procedure exits.
The CATCH returns error text as a result set without rethrowing or returning a failure status.
The negative OrderID check uses RAISERROR rather than THROW.
PRINT sends a buffered text message rather than a structured diagnostic.
The query is fixed to customer ID 1.
The OrderDate filter embeds an unexplained January 1, 2016 cutoff.
Without a conversion style, '01/02/2016' can mean January 2 or February 1 depending on session settings.
TOP (1) does not specify which order matching an invoice to return.
COALESCE wraps both indexed CustomerID columns even though both are NOT NULL, which can impede direct index use.
The self-join query returns an arbitrary order ID.
Joining Orders to itself on its primary key adds no data or filtering.
Sorting all orders by the nvarchar(max) Comments column can consume substantial memory and spill to tempdb.
SUM(Quantity) processes all Sales.OrderLines rows without a restrictive filter.
OrderID > 0 filters a grouping key and can be applied in WHERE before grouping.
COUNT(*) must count all Sales.Orders rows because the query has no restrictive filter.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns one row, so ordering by OrderCount has no effect.
MERGE adds complexity to a matched-only operation on Sales.Orders that does not require an upsert.
The MERGE assigns Comments to itself, potentially taking write locks or firing triggers without changing the value.
Updating Comments to its current value can still take write locks and fire triggers.
The DELETE can remove every order line with Quantity = -1 across all orders.
The DELETE depends on an unexplained quantity sentinel of -1.
WAITFOR DELAY pauses the session and ties up a worker during the wait.
The transaction starts outside a TRY/CATCH boundary, so the procedure has no local error handler for it.
IDENTITY_INSERT requires an identity column, but the supplied Sales.Orders definition has none.
The call to sp_who omits the sys schema.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset within the procedure and can cap later SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements at one row.
The VALUES insert depends on the declared column order of #DemoCategories.
The insert assigns a fixed CategoryID of 99.
Prefixing @CustomerName with '%' prevents a prefix seek on the CustomerName index.
The procedure concatenates caller-controlled @CustomerName directly into executable SQL; bind the LIKE pattern as a parameter instead.
The call to sp_executesql omits the sys schema.
The UPDATE has no predicate to identify intended customers; with ROWCOUNT 1 still active, it can change an arbitrary qualifying row.
The update assigns a fixed CustomerCategoryID of 1.
Filtering o.OrderDate in WHERE discards customers with no matching order, defeating the LEFT JOIN.
The order filter embeds an unexplained January 1, 2016 cutoff.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL does not test for nulls; the comparison evaluates to UNKNOWN under ANSI NULL semantics.
dbo.GetCustomerType can execute once per returned customer unless SQL Server can inline it.
If the DELETE or COMMIT fails and the transaction remains active, the CATCH does not roll it back.
The CATCH returns error text but does not signal that the transactional operation failed.
INDEX = 1 forces the clustered index and prevents the optimizer from choosing the CustomerName index.
Three derived-table layers merely repeat CustomerID and can be flattened into the innermost query.
LIKE '%A%' cannot use a prefix seek on the CustomerName index.
The result exposes every column returned by dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti, coupling callers to its full output schema.
If dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement TVF as its name suggests, its table result can limit cardinality estimation and optimization; verify the function definition.
